extraction.name: SeamlessM4T: Massively Multilingual & Multimodal Machine Translation
extraction.description: SeamlessM4T is a single model that supports speech-to-speech translation, speech-to-text translation, text-to-speech translation, text-to-text translation, and automatic speech recognition for up to 100 languages. To build this, 1 million hours of open speech audio data were used to learn self-supervised speech representations with w2v-BERT 2.0. Subsequently, a multimodal corpus of automatically aligned speech translations, dubbed SeamlessAlign, was created. Filtered and combined with human-labeled and pseudo-labeled data (totaling 406,000 hours), the first multilingual system capable of translating from and into English for both speech and text was developed. SeamlessM4T sets a new standard for translations into multiple target languages, achieving an improvement of 20% BLEU over the previous state-of-the-art in direct speech-to-text translation. Compared to strong cascaded models, SeamlessM4T improves the quality of into-English translation by 1.3 BLEU points in speech-to-text and by 2.6 ASR-BLEU points in speech-to-speech. Preliminary human evaluations of speech-to-text translation outputs evinced similarly impressive results; for translations from English, XSTS scores for 24 evaluated languages are consistently above 4 (out of 5). The system was evaluated for robustness against background noises and speaker variations, performing better with average improvements of 38% and 49% respectively in speech-to-text tasks. SeamlessM4T was also evaluated on gender bias and added toxicity, reporting up to 63% reduction in added toxicity in translation outputs compared to the state-of-the-art. All contributions, including models, inference code, finetuning recipes, and metadata to recreate the unfiltered 470,000 hours of SeamlessAlign, are open-sourced.

extraction.rai:dataCollection: The SeamlessAlign corpus was created using parallel data mining. This involved starting with a large collection of raw audio, chunking files into overlapping segments, and applying speech Language Identification (LID). On the text side, a sentence-segmented dataset drawn from NLLB was used. Speech and text corpora were then projected into a common embedding space (SONAR), in which mining was performed to identify translation pairs with optimal segmentation. Improvements over the original SpeechMatrix pipeline include an improved and extended speech language identification (LID) model, a novel multimodal embedding space, increased coverage from 17 to 37 languages, and increased raw audio amount, totaling 4 million hours. The mining was focused on 37 target languages of the SeamlessM4T system.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Software Collection, Secondary Data analysis
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: 1 million hours of open speech audio data for self-supervised speech representations. 4 million hours of raw audio originating from a publicly available repository of crawled web data. Sentence-segmented dataset drawn from NLLB. Human-labeled and pseudo-labeled data totaling 406,000 hours. Human-performed ASR transcriptions.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Text pre-processing: The same data sources, cleaning, and filtering steps as NLLB were used and run at scale with the Stopes library. Audio pre-processing: Audio file URLs were deduplicated, files downloaded, and resampled at 16KHz. Non-speech data was filtered out with a bespoke audio event detection (AED) model. Audio segmentation: An open Voice Activity Detection (VAD) model was used to split audio files into shorter segments. A speech LID model was used on each file. Several possible overlapping splits of each segment were created, with the optimal split chosen by the mining algorithm. Filtering: Additional filtering was performed on the combined pool of primary and mined data, including a toxicity filter to remove pairs with toxicity imbalance, a length filter (utterance shorter than 0.1s or longer than 50s, text longer than 250 sub-words), and removal of pairs where text contains more than 20% emojis, 50% punctuations, or 50% spaces. Discrete acoustic units: Features were extracted from the 35th layer of XLS-R-1B for continuous speech representations. A k-means algorithm was applied to these representations to estimate 10,000 cluster centroids to map to discrete acoustic units.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human-labeled data was combined with pseudo-labeled data. ASR data was pseudo-labeled using a multilingual T2TT model (NLLB-200-3.3B). Multilingual text-to-unit (T2U) models were trained on ASR datasets to directly convert text into target discrete units for pseudo-labeling S2ST data.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: For human evaluation, 3 annotators examined each source-target audio pair (or audio-text pair) and evaluated semantic similarity using the XSTS protocol. In cases of disagreement (score values of 2 or more), 2 additional annotators evaluated the item (totaling 5 scores). The median score was taken. Scores were calibrated using the ‘moderated calibration’ methodology with a cross-lingual calibration set to reduce language-level annotator biases.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 3 to 5 human annotators per item for XSTS evaluation.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: All annotators who worked on the human evaluation of detected toxicity are team members who are aware of the toxic nature of the samples prior to analyzing them.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: NLLB-200-3.3B (for pseudo-labeling ASR data), multilingual text-to-unit (T2U) models (for pseudo-labeling S2ST data), Whisper-Large-v2 and Whisper-Medium (for ASR-BLEU evaluation), ETOX (for toxicity detection), MMS-TTS (for speech extension of Multilingual HolisticBias dataset).
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Metadata to recreate the unfiltered 470,000 hours of SeamlessAlign are open-sourced at https://github.com/facebookresearch/seamless_communication, allowing the community to rebuild and use it for their own purposes. The optimal threshold for mining can be tuned based on the task, balancing dataset size and alignment quality. The mining code is also open-sourced in the Stopes library.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Personally identifiable information may not be entirely eliminated from the training data. Gender information is collected and analyzed for bias evaluation.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The model aims to facilitate and streamline multilingual contact online and offline, augmenting 'world-readiness' by lowering barriers in cross-lingual communication. It can support users in multilingual conversations and boost confidence in speech-heavy interactions. It is particularly beneficial for inclusion and accessibility for individuals who lack reading or writing skills, are blind or visually impaired, or whose languages have multiple writing systems, providing access to information and communication in a more natural and dynamic manner. It may also be instrumental in preventing endangerment for languages without standardized writing systems.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The model was evaluated for gender bias and added toxicity. SeamlessM4T overgeneralizes to masculine forms when translating from neutral terms (average preference of ~10%) and shows a lack of robustness when varying gender (~3%). Gender representation analysis revealed an overrepresentation of masculine lexica compared to feminine in analyzed datasets. ASR performance may vary based on gender, race, accent, or language.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The Fleurs test set is limited by slightly different sets of sentences across language pairs and a lack of speaker diversity. Human evaluation is limited by small annotator sample sizes (typically 3 per sentence) and potential human biases (e.g., recency bias). Word list-based toxicity detection (ETOX) has limitations: tendency to over-detect context-dependent toxic terms, reliance on precise tokenization (difficult for non-segmenting languages), and ASR before lexical matching can lead to false negatives. Noun lists for gender imbalance detection share word list limitations and rely on linguistic gender clues as a proxy. The model is a research model, not for production deployment, and not intended for domain-specific inputs (e.g., medical, legal) or long-form translation, as quality may degrade. Translations cannot be used as certified translations. ASR performance may vary based on gender, race, accent, or language, and translation of slang or proper nouns may be inconsistent across high and low-resource languages. S2ST may carry higher interactional risks due to immediate reception and feedback compared to written language.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Primary intended uses are research in speech and text translation, including Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Speech-to-Speech Translation (S2ST), Speech-to-Text Translation (S2TT), Text-to-Speech Translation (T2ST), Text-to-Text Translation (T2TT), and Text-to-Speech (TTS). It is suitable for Training, Testing, Validation, and Fine Tuning. Usage guidelines recommend viewing SeamlessM4T-fueled applications as an augmentation device that assists in translation rather than a tool that replaces the need for language learning or reliable human interpreters, especially in high-stakes situations involving legal or medical decision-making.
